overview: StoneCo Ltd. is a Cayman Islands-domiciled fintech holding company whose operating business serves micro, small, and medium-sized Brazilian merchants (MSMBs) and larger accounts through an integrated platform spanning payments/merchant acquiring, digital banking (Conta Stone), and SMB credit. The company went public on Nasdaq in 2018, built its moat around hyper-local distribution ("Stone Hubs" and "Green Angels"), proprietary technology, and high-touch customer service, and in 2026 completed the divestment of its Linx retail-software business to TOTVS to refocus entirely on the payments-banking-credit "financial platform" strategy for Brazilian entrepreneurs.

business_model.summary: Stone earns revenue primarily from merchant discount rate (MDR) fees and related transaction/subscription revenue on card and Pix payment volume (TPV), supplemented by financial income from receivables prepayment (anticipation) and float on client balances, plus a fast-growing credit business (working capital loans and credit cards to merchants) and banking products (digital accounts, deposits). Following the 2026 sale of Linx, software/ERP revenue has been discontinued from ongoing operations, leaving a 'payments + banking + credit' model built on proprietary merchant transaction data for underwriting.

revenue_streams.name: Net revenue from transaction activities and other services (MDR/issuer)

business_model.customer_type: B2B/SMB — micro, small and medium Brazilian merchants (MSMB) across Stone and Ton brands, plus a smaller Large Accounts segment; software (Linx) customers divested in 2026
business_model.geographic_mix: Brazil only (100% of revenue); USD-based investors bear full BRL/USD translation exposure since all operations and functional currency are Brazilian real

competitive_position.market_position: Independent acquirer with roughly 15-20% share of Brazilian card-acquiring volume, strongest among MSMB merchants; the five largest acquirers (Cielo, Rede, Stone, PagBank, Getnet) together process the large majority of card TPV. In banking/credit, Stone's digital account and lending book are far smaller in scale than Nubank's tens of millions of retail customers or Mercado Pago's wallet-driven ecosystem.

moat_factors.description: Proprietary 'Stone Hub' network and locally-based sales/support agents ('Green Angels') give fast, high-touch service that is difficult for centralized bank-owned acquirers to replicate, though digital-first competitors (Nubank, Mercado Pago) sidestep this advantage with app-based acquisition.

Access to real-time merchant sales data allows differentiated credit underwriting versus traditional banks, though the 2021-2022 and 2025-2026 credit cycles show this edge has not prevented material delinquency spikes.

End-to-end owned processing/gateway/banking stack (no reliance on third-party core banking or processing) supports bundling of payments, banking and credit, improving unit economics as clients adopt more products.
Historically high Net Promoter Scores versus incumbent bank-owned acquirers, though this is being tested by elevated churn in the Ton brand since 4Q25.
MDR pricing is highly commoditized and portable; switching costs rise only as merchants adopt banking/credit alongside payments, which is still a minority of the base.

weaknesses: Thin/declining differentiation in core card-acquiring, which is intensely price-competitive and subject to continuous MDR/prepayment repricing
Small scale relative to bank-owned giants (Itaú/Rede, Santander/Getnet, Bradesco/Cielo) that can cross-subsidize acquiring with balance-sheet and distribution advantages

Credit book is young (more than doubled YoY in 2025-2026) and has shown rising NPLs (15-90 day NPL up from ~2.5% to 6.0% YoY as of 2Q26; >90 day NPL up to 8.6%), raising doubts about underwriting durability through a full credit cycle
History of volume/client-base deceleration and elevated churn in the Ton micro-merchant brand since 4Q25
No meaningful presence outside Brazil, leaving no geographic diversification

growth_drivers: Expansion and deepening of the merchant credit book (working capital loans, credit cards), which more than doubled year-over-year and is now a major contributor to revenue growth
Cross-sell of banking products (retail/time deposits, Conta Stone) funding a lower-cost deposit base and deepening wallet share per merchant (ARPAC)
Initiatives to reduce elevated Ton-brand churn via bundled/simplified offerings, showing early positive traction in 2026
Pix QR Code acceptance growth (+44% YoY in 2Q26) as a new, lower-cost transaction channel embedded into Stone's merchant offering
Continued large-scale share buybacks (R$3.0bn over the twelve months to 2Q26) mechanically growing per-share metrics as the float shrinks
AI-driven productivity initiatives in customer support, engineering and operations aimed at structurally lowering the cost base
Post-Linx simplification sharpening management focus and capital exclusively on the payments-banking-credit 'financial platform' strategy for Brazilian entrepreneurs
Brazil's still-low penetration of electronic payments, credit cards and digital financial services relative to developed markets, providing a long secular runway

business.description: Bank-owned acquirers (Cielo, Rede, Getnet) and well-capitalized fintech rivals (Nubank, Mercado Pago, PagBank) compete aggressively on MDR and bundled banking/credit offers, pressuring take rates and client retention.
Churn rose notably from 4Q25, concentrated in the Ton micro-merchant brand; management's remediation is early-stage and unproven at scale, especially for larger/more complex merchants.

NPL 15-90 days and >90 days both roughly doubled to tripled year-over-year through 2Q26, driven by weaker 2H25/early-2026 vintages and specific large-ticket ('dedicated desk') delinquencies; coverage ratio has fallen from ~280% to ~204% even as the book keeps growing fast.
Revenue is entirely dependent on the health of Brazilian micro and small businesses, a segment highly sensitive to domestic economic cycles.

financial.risk: Funding cost exposure to Brazilian interest rates
financial.description: Financial expenses (funding prepayment/credit book) are directly linked to the CDI rate; a higher-for-longer Selic (~14-15%) compresses margins and was cited as the reason management guided toward the low end of 2026 targets.

All revenue and earnings are generated and reported in Brazilian reais; BRL depreciation directly reduces USD-equivalent value of earnings, dividends and buybacks regardless of underlying BRL performance.

Scaling the credit book consumes capital and net cash (net cash position fell from R$4.7bn to roughly R$2.6bn year-over-year as of 4Q25), constraining the pace of future buybacks if credit losses accelerate.

regulatory.risk: Banco Central do Brasil (BCB) regulatory changes
regulatory.description: The BCB continues to actively regulate payment institutions, Pix, interchange/MDR caps on debit transactions, and anti-money-laundering requirements (e.g., Circular 3,978-style updates); new minimum capital requirements for Pix-enabled institutions are being phased in from mid-2026 through 2028.

Brazil's free, instant Pix payment rail (now also expanding into QR-code acceptance, installments and escrow features) continues to divert transaction volume away from traditional card rails over time, though Stone has so far monetized Pix QR acceptance rather than being purely disrupted by it.

regulatory.risk: Securities litigation / legacy class action exposure
regulatory.description: StoneCo settled a U.S. securities class action (R$145.3 million, ~R$96.6 million insurance-covered) related to the former credit product and the 2021 fair-value write-down; residual legal/governance risk remains from that episode.

macro.risk: Brazilian interest rate and credit cycle sensitivity
macro.description: Both funding costs and merchant credit demand/delinquency are highly sensitive to the Selic rate cycle; the current higher-for-longer rate environment is a direct headwind to 2026 guidance.

Consumption, SMB formation and payment volumes are tied to Brazilian GDP growth, inflation, and political stability; recession or policy shocks would compress TPV growth and credit quality simultaneously.
Historical BRL/USD volatility (e.g., 20%+ annual swings) directly affects USD-denominated valuation of the stock independent of operating performance.

macro_factors.industry_outlook: Brazilian electronic payments and SMB fintech penetration remain structurally below developed-market levels (lower card/credit card penetration, lower e-commerce penetration historically), supporting multi-year volume growth, but the acquiring segment has matured and pricing power has eroded as incumbents and fintechs converge on bundled banking-plus-credit models.
macro_factors.cyclicality: Moderately cyclical — payment volumes track consumer/SMB spending, and the newer credit business is directly exposed to the Brazilian credit cycle (delinquency rises sharply when rates are high and growth slows)
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: High — Brazilian benchmark (Selic/CDI) rates directly set funding costs for prepayment/credit financing and heavily influence prepayment/float revenue and merchant credit demand and delinquency

recent_developments.event: StoneCo announced the divestment of Linx and related software assets to TOTVS for an enterprise value of ~R$3.05 billion (~R$3.4 billion including net cash), refocusing the company on payments, banking and credit.
Closing of the Linx divestment to TOTVS was completed; StoneCo recognized an additional R$157.8 million impairment in 4Q25 related to revised fair-value assumptions on the disposal group.

4Q25/FY2025 results reported: full-year adjusted gross profit of R$6.3bn (+13.5% YoY) and adjusted basic EPS of R$9.71 (+33.6% YoY); announced CEO transition with Pedro Zinner moving to non-executive Chairman and CFO Mateus Scherer becoming CEO.
Securities class action settlement related to the former credit product approved by the court for R$145.3 million (R$96.6 million covered by insurers).
Paid an extraordinary cash dividend of US$2.53 per share (Class A and Class B), totaling ~R$3.08 billion, funded by Linx sale proceeds.

2Q26 results showed total revenue of R$3.59bn (+2.5% YoY), adjusted EPS of R$2.40 (+8.6% YoY) aided by buybacks, but credit NPLs rose sharply (15-90 day NPL to 6.00% from 2.51% YoY; >90 day NPL to 8.60% from 4.67% YoY) and a R$200+ million non-recurring IFRS provision was booked for allowances on card issuers in distress.

Morgan Stanley reiterated an Underweight/Sell rating with a $9 price target, citing the slowest-ever payment volume growth alongside rapidly rising credit delinquency; other brokers (UBS, JPMorgan) maintained Buy ratings with targets near $17.
Company disclosed elevated merchant churn beginning in 4Q25, concentrated in the Ton micro-merchant brand, prompting bundled-offer and pricing initiatives that showed early improvement by 2Q26.

items.notes: Narrowed from an initial R$4.6-7.0 billion-type range toward the lower end due to a higher-for-longer Selic rate (~14%) versus the ~12.5% initially assumed, creating an estimated BRL 300+ million headwind.
Management explicitly guided to deliver toward the lower end of the range given macro headwinds; buybacks remain a key lever supporting EPS growth above net income growth.

items.target: trending down to high-teens percent by year-end 2026
items.notes: Management expects cost of risk (currently ~21.5%) to improve as government-backed, lower-risk credit lines are mixed into the portfolio and as weaker 2H25/early-2026 vintages season through.

items.target: continued large buybacks; ~30% shareholder yield referenced by analysts for 2026
items.notes: Framework: reinvest where returns exceed cost of capital, maintain credit buffers, and return excess capital via buybacks; R$3.0 billion repurchased over the twelve months to 2Q26, reducing share count by 40.3 million shares.

guidance.management_commentary: New CEO Mateus Scherer has emphasized 'high-quality growth and capital efficiency' and balancing growth with caution in credit. Management has been explicit that TPV growth deliberately decelerated in 2025 rather than 'chasing volume that does not compound,' and that Ton-focused churn-reduction initiatives are showing early but not yet fully scaled results. The company continues to frame 2026 as a year of executing with discipline following the 2025 'simplification' (Linx sale) and leadership transition.

bull_case: Credit and banking cross-sell into an already large (~4.8 million) active merchant base provides a long runway to lift ARPAC well above pure-payments levels, with the credit book still small relative to the merchant base and doubling+ year-over-year

Aggressive capital return (large buybacks funded by Linx sale proceeds and ongoing free cash flow) is shrinking the share count meaningfully, amplifying per-share earnings growth even if absolute profit growth is modest

Post-Linx simplification sharpens management focus and capital allocation purely on the core payments-banking-credit 'financial platform' strategy, with a credible, continuity-oriented leadership transition (long-tenured CFO promoted to CEO)
Valuation is low on a trailing basis (single-digit trailing P/E, high-teens ROE) relative to growth, if credit losses normalize as government-backed, lower-risk lending mixes into the portfolio
Structural secular tailwind from continued under-penetration of digital payments, credit cards and SMB lending in Brazil relative to developed markets
bear_case: Core payments business is decelerating — 2Q26 TPV growth of ~3-4% YoY is among the slowest on record, with elevated merchant churn (especially in the Ton brand) only partially addressed by recent bundling initiatives

Credit portfolio delinquency is rising quickly just as the book scales rapidly: 15-90 day NPL roughly doubled and >90 day NPL nearly doubled year-over-year through 2Q26, while coverage ratio has fallen, raising doubts about underwriting discipline in only the book's second year of aggressive growth — echoing the 2021 credit/collateral crisis that previously crashed the stock
Direct exposure to Brazil's higher-for-longer Selic/CDI rate environment compresses margins and funding economics and has already forced management to guide toward the low end of 2026 targets

Intensifying competition from both bank-owned acquirers (Cielo, Rede, Getnet) with balance-sheet scale and digital-native rivals (Nubank, Mercado Pago) with large, low-cost-of-acquisition customer bases threatens to permanently compress Stone's take rates and market share

100% Brazil/BRL revenue concentration means USD-based investors bear full currency and sovereign macro risk, and the company carries reputational overhang from its 2021 fair-value write-down and subsequent securities class action settlement
